replying_to: Replying to Neuro-Symbolic Ontology-Mediated Query Answering
display_title: Official Review of Paper2448 by Reviewer cmg7

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors study the problem of ontology-mediated query answering (OMQA) over knowledge graphs (KGs). The problem definition is as follows: given an ontology,  an incomplete KG, and a monadic (positive) conjunctive query (CQ) which does not have a match in the given KG, predict/rank/score the most likely answers to the query. The proposed approach largely builds on existing work of Query2Box on answering monadic CQs over incomplete KGs, while extending this approach to make the embeddings, and hence their predictions, "ontology-aware".
content.main_review:
*Strengths:*

The problem is meaningful, essentially importing the idea of OMQA to the domain of embedding-based approaches: one is interested in query answering over incomplete KGs using an embedding-based approach, while additionally making use of a logical background theory. This is commonly referred as rule injection in the context of KG embedding models. It is widely studied for, e.g., link prediction - performing link prediction while incorporating a set of given rules. 

*Weaknesses:*

While the problem formulation is meaningful, the presented study appears rather shallow both theoretically and empirically. After describing the problem setup, authors state the following alternatives for solving the task: 
1. Train existing embedding models for logical QA on the data derived from the deductive closure of $G$ instead of $G$;
2. Develop an ontology-aware embedding model that will be trained on $G$, but will have special terms in the training objective structurally enforcing $O$.

There is an obvious alternative which is completely missed: consider existing embedding models developed for link prediction, which possess rule injection capacity (i.e., can inject (subset of) rules of $O$) and train these following (Arakelyan et al., 2021)  for QA. The resulting model will be ontology-aware by construction, though disjoint from approaches (1) and (2). For example, BoxE can inject all rules from Fig 5 excluding (5). Since by (Arakelyan et al., 2021) it is possible to turn any link prediction model to a QA answering model, one would obtain an ontology-aware QA model. It is easy to see that this approach would result in much stronger baselines that the ones provided and so the presented results cannot be conclusive without such an analysis. Hence, the empirical evaluation is limited. Besides, I had a hard time to understand the experimental setup and the results are not discussed in detail: In many instances, it is not clear to me what to make out of these results, and there is generally a lack of insights.

This work is very incremental on Query2Box and lacks novelty.  The authors only modify the loss function and the query sampling strategy. In my understanding the main challenge in this approach is to incorporate the rules and there is a large body of work on this. While support for rules is generally limited, this work does not offer anything new in this respect either. In fact, the whole approach uses the Query2Box for model representation which itself has limitations in incorporating rules. It is possible to come up with examples, where Query2Box would fail to inject the intended meaning of the rules, and the current paper does not add anything new in this respect and neither does it include a formal analysis discussing their limitations.

Another obvious problem with the current approach is that it follows Query2Box approach and so is based on query sampling. (Arakelyan et al., 2021) obtain state-of-the-art results by using a simple framework requiring only neural link predictors trained for atomic queries, rather than millions of queries as in Query2Box. I could not find any strong arguments to justify a query sampling approach which comes with many additional problems/challenges. 

Some minor issues:

- A knowledge graph is not the same as an ABox. There are semantic differences. (I understand what authors mean here, but it is misleading).
- The presented monadic CQs are actually monadic positive CQs.
- In Prelim's X is a variable, and $\vec{Y}$ is a sequence of variables, and their union is not well-defined.
- In Def 1, the term "ideal completion" is undefined.
- In Def 1, ontology-awareness is not well defined (one direction of iff is missing)?
content.summary_of_the_review: In light of the major weaknesses listed in my review, I recommend reject.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2448 by Reviewer cmg7

content.title: Answer for cmg7
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for the constructive feedback. We want to point out that our contributions go beyond the mentioned ones.

Alternatives for OMQA over embeddings: Apart from the mentioned two cases we also consider the query rewriting-based approach, in which a query is rewritten into a union of CQs, which are executed over pre-trained embedding models (see E2 on p. 15). In the classical setting, this approach is the preferred one, since the materialization is in general costly, however, in the case of KGEs such an approach is not the most effective.
Ontology-driven query sampling is useful in capturing the relevant information in the graph without the need to consider all triples. As our experiments show for LUBM, CQD_onto is trained using considerably fewer triples than CQD_plain. In cases when the KG is very large, query sampling would be more suitable than training on a complete set of triples. 
We created 2 benchmarks for evaluating the capabilities of an embedding-based QA model to perform inductive and deductive reasoning. 

We address each particular comment below.


> Regarding the alternative approach, i.e. CQD + BoxE

We agree that the combination of BoxE and CQD is an alternative. However, incorporating existing BoxE implementation into CQD  is not straightforward, since e.g. concept inclusion axioms like $(X, \text{type}, a) \Rightarrow (X, \text{type}, b)$ are not explicitly supported, as well as rules containing constants (see Table 1 in https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.06267). Furthermore, a closer comparison between BoxE (https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.06267) and ComplEx+N3 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07297), the neural link predictor used by CQD, shows that BoxE produces significantly less accurate results across the board.

For this reason, we are now incorporating Adversarial Set Regularisation (https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.07596), a neural link predictor-independent rule injection method, to incorporate logic rules in the link predictor used by CQD.


Moreover, please note that training on queries has the advantage in the inference phase: answers to queries can be computed efficiently. This is in contrast with CQD, in which computing answers could be computationally expensive, e.g. due to Beam-search.  This leads to a trade-off between precomputation (training) time and constant query evaluation time. Moreover, query-based training captures more expressive ontology languages and in particular, our model O2B is easily adaptable for such cases.  


We do not see why CQD + BoxE would clearly lead to a better baseline since, in our opinion, it depends very much on the performance of the used link predictors. Could you please elaborate on that?


> Regarding lack of novelty

As far as we know there is no prior work on embedding-based OMQ answering. Our work formalises such a problem and shows that it is, at the moment, challenging for state-of-the-art embedding-based QA models. We believe that this work addresses such shortcomings and opens the way for alternative neuro-symbolic solutions. 


> Regarding lack of insights

One of the major insights of our work is that embedding-based QA models, when used out of the box, are not well-suited for Ontology-mediated QA, even when the ontology language is not very expressive (such as DL-Lite). As shown by the extensive body of work to answer OMQs in the classical KR approach, such a problem is challenging and requires well-crafted solutions that depend on ontology expressiveness. We think that such a problem is non-trivial also in the case of KGEs.


> Regarding main challenge and incorporating rules in Query2Box

The main challenge is to perform inductive+deductive reasoning to obtain complete answers to queries, not just for link prediction (1-hop queries). Such a task requires the application of rules over missing edges in the KG. Our focus is on DL-Lite; however, similar training strategies and training objectives can be obtained also for other ontology languages. Note that DL-Lite has existential rules, which are not supported in other methods, e.g. BoxE.

> Regarding the example of rules with r,s1,s2

We do not see why the case illustrated, e.g., in https://ibb.co/F7kx2Yt will not be supported by our method. This does not enforce s1 implies s2 or vice versa as in your comment. Could you please elaborate on that?

content.title: Final comments
content.comment:
Thanks for all the answers. My general concerns remain after going through your answers, but let me briefly clarify a few things you asked for:

- I am not suggesting to dismiss alternative approaches by pointing to (Arakelyan et al., 2021) - In fact, I think there are weaknesses with the approach presented in (Arakelyan et al., 2021), but the issue is about the respective advantages and disadvantages of each approach. In my opinion, the query sampling approach you take is very problematic, especially with ontologies (see also my point below). 

- While this works extends Query2Box, it adds really very little to it technically, or conceptually. Most importantly, there is generally a lack of formal analysis: Query2Box has well-known limitations which will impact your work. That being said, my earlier example for Query2Box is not correct (it is for GQE actually) but it is well-known that Query2Box cannot handle cycles over variables, i.e.,  even queries containing atoms $s(x,y) \land t(y,x)$ cannot be handled in Query2Box and DL-Lite can easily introduce such dependencies. Since you eventually use the Query2Box space, you are necessarily subject to such limitations (and many others). In any case, as I stated in my original review, these need to be analysed carefully and my point goes beyond an individual example or a model. 

-  In the paper, you stated that there are two alternatives for solving the task and I opposed this in my review, and mentioned that any model with rule injection capacity can be used as an alternative. I am glad we agreed here.

content.title: Final reply
content.comment:
Thank you for the reply. Our final remarks are stated below:

1. We totally agree that both of the considered approaches CQD and Query2box have their limitations; the purpose of our work is not to propose yet another model but to build upon/adapt state-of-the-art techniques to perform OMQA over incomplete KGs. 
Moreover, as mentioned in our previous comments, the proposed solutions, in particular the training objective and ontology-driven training sampling, are generic enough to be applied to other query-based embedding models. As this is the first attempt to embedding-based OMQA we also propose methods to empirically evaluate the effectiveness which go beyond the chosen model. 
2. Handling cyclic queries have been known to be very challenging even in classical OMQA. We agree that there are limitations regarding the form of supported queries in Query2Box, but neither Query2Box nor existing embedding-based QA approaches support OMQA, to our best knowledge. Additionally, please note that DL-Lite cannot introduce cyclic dependencies as you mentioned: each query atom gets rewritten, based on some applicable axiom, and the result is a unique atom; moreover the variables are carefully handled during such a process. Thus, if the original query is cycle-free so is the resulting rewritten query.
3. We agree that your suggestion is an alternative but it does not mean that one can easily plug-in any of such models and expect that it results “in much stronger baselines” as you pointed out. Please also note that none of the existing models with rule injection can allow existential rules (i.e, constructor $\exists r. \top$) as supported in DL-Lite. This is an important feature in many applications [Artale et al.].

[1] The DL-Lite Family and Relations. Alessandro Artale, Diego Calvanese, Roman Kontchakov, Michael Zakharyaschev

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2448 by Reviewer cmg7

content.title: Answer for cmg7, part 2
content.comment:
> Regarding the query sampling process

We agree that the method by Arakelyan et al. is an elegant way to do query answering. However, this should not be used to ignore all query sampling approaches. As mentioned before, query sampling-based approaches offer some advantages such as constant time query evaluation and adaptability to various ontology languages. We do not think they should be dismissed in the case of OMQA.  What we propose in this paper is applicable to many region-based KG embeddings. 
For example, via the query inclusion technique, one can inject more complex axioms than those supported by the existing methods (e.g., BoxE). Indeed, consider a pair of queries: q1(Y):- nationality(X,”Canadian”), hasAward(X,”TuringAward”), graduatedFrom(X,Y) and q2(Y):- nationality(X,”American”), worksFor(X,”Google”), hasPhDFrom(X,Y). Using our method one can enforce the following complex rule: “The set of universities, from which Canadian Turing Awardees are graduated is included in the set of universities from which American Google employees got their PhDs degrees”.  To the best of our knowledge, existing embedding methods cannot capture this kind of complex rules involving constants.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2448 by Reviewer YwJs

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes ontology mediated Neuro symbolic query answering system that uses popular embeddings and knowledge present in the ontology to bring the inductive and deductive reasoning capabilities for query answering.  
Paper proposes strategies to use ontology axioms to improve embedding training for both query based embedding methods and atom based embedding methods. Authors introduce two new benchmarks where this can be tested and show 
positive results that can be obtained on queries that span across deductive, inductive and inductive+ deductive scenarios
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
1. Paper explores how inductive and deductive reasoning capabilities can be integrated in knowledge graph query answering. 
2. Paper is well motivated and the approach is described clearly.
3. Paper proposes ways to generate training data to cover different aspects of the deductive reasoning.
4. Describes ontology aware training objective description that can be easily incorporated into existing embedding methods(Q2B and O2B) and show it two existing methods.
5. Benchmark datasets creation methodology and the two datasets introduced based on LUBM and NELL can be useful to the research community in pushing complex query answering research.
Weakness:
 1. Experimental results on newly introduced modification O2B by modifying Q2B does’t seem to yield consistent results across all the scenarios. Any insights around this ?
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall the paper is well written with new benchmarks and novel way to do query answering to support deductive and inductive reasoning. 
Initial experimental results show good gains for the new benchmarks and scenarios introduced. 
This will open up new research to push the inductive and inductive reasoning for KG embedding methods.

content.title: Answer for YwJs
content.comment:
Thank you for the encouraging feedback.

Regarding our experimental results, we compare the Q2B_plain baseline with our best performing model, O2B_onto, and we observe rather consistent improvements. Indeed, for example, on LUBM in the most challenging inductive + deductive case (I+D), we obtain 0.218 for Q2B_plain and 0.707 for O2B_onto. We observe similar results on the NELL dataset.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2448 by Reviewer 3TPL

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper targets a problem about formal query answering over an incomplete knowledge graph with a background DL-Lite_R ontology, where the formal queries are restricted to certain shapes. The paper extends existing methods for embedding query answering over knowledge graph without background ontology, namely Query2Box (Ren et al. 2020) and CQD (Arakelyan et al. 2021), with data sampling and a revised training objective. To cope with the background ontology, the basic idea for data sampling is to sample queries rewritten from the given query to train the embedding model, whereas the main revision to the training objective is to consider all queries generalized from the given query. The paper also provides two new datasets (LUBM and NELL) for the targeting problem and presents evaluation on Query2Box, CQD and their extensions mentioned above.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
(1) The paper provides two new datasets for the problem about formal query answering over an incomplete knowledge graph with a background DL-Lite_R ontology.
(2) The paper also proposes two main extensions to enhance a method for embedding query answering to cope with background ontology.

Weaknesses:
(1) The usage of generalizations of a query will enlarge the set of certain answers to the query. In fact, all queries rewritten from a query based on a background ontology are specializations (from the right-hand side of the subsumption to the left-hand side), and thus the exact set of certain answers can be preserved. It is very unclear why generalizations are used in both data sampling and the revised training objective. In other words, the design of the extensions is questionable.
(2) There are no evident implications from the main experimental results (see Figure 4 and Table 2); in particular, there is lack of evidence that the extensions are effective in improving the baseline methods Query2Box (Q2B) and CQD. If I do not misunderstand, the method O2B is enhanced from Q2B with the proposed extensions. However, O2B is inferior to Q2B in two (LUBM gen and LUBM spec) out of eight cases; i.e., the extensions are not effective in these cases. It is said in the paper that the proposed solution (O2B?) improves Q2B for almost 50% and CQD for almost 54% in terms of LUBM I+D, and that it improves Q2B for almost 20% and CQD for almost 25% in terms of NELL. However, these improvements cannot be checked from Figure 4 or Table 2. In contrast, CQD_gen and CQD_spec outperforms O2B_any a lot according to Figure 4 and Table 2.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has marginal novelty on two extensions of an embedding method for query answering. Both extensions rely on generalizations of a given query which may enlarge the set of certain answers to the query. This design of extensions is questionable and have not been addressed in the paper. The evaluation is insufficient to show that the proposed extensions are effective in improving the baseline methods Query2Box (Q2B) and CQD.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2448 by Reviewer 3TPL

content.title: Answer for 3TPL
content.comment:
Thank you for the useful feedback.

Regarding weakness (1), we chose generalizations because they guarantee the creation of queries that have answers and for the training objective, the specializations would limit the applicability of rules. For example, if the ontology contains Student(X) -> Person(X), and we have the query q(X):- Student(X) as the training query, the specializations would miss the information that each student is a person, while if we have q(X):- Person(X) as the training query, it might be that the specialized query q(X):- Student(X) does not have any answers. Note that, during training, only queries that have answers are selected. Moreover, in our experiments, we do consider a training case in which we incorporate the specializations but this does not lead to better results (see the beginning of p. 9). The above observations motivated our design of the training objective using generalizations.

Regarding (2), the baselines we consider are Q2B_plain and CQD_plain (see Models and Datasets paragraph on p. 8), and our best performing models are O2B_onto and CQD_gen/CQD_onto. Comparing the results of the respective models we obtain mentioned improvements.
